in_text_mentions: The anorectal angle, depth of rectocele, and perineum descending images via the defecation proctography method are shown in Figure 3. Compared to the sitting position, participants in the squatting position showed a larger degree of anorectal angle at rest (P = 0.023) and during contraction (P < 0.001), maximal Valsalva (P < 0.001), and evacuation (P < 0.001); a deeper depth of rectocele at maximal Valsalva (P < 0.001) and evacuation (P = 0.004); and a longer length of perineum descending during contraction (P = 0.002) and maximal Valsalva (P = 0.022) (Table 1).

findings.label: Anterior rectal wall intussusception on defecography

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (a, b). a: Sagittal MRI defecography at rest shows mild posterior compartment descent; in-text associates this figure with a small anterior rectocele, supporting rectocele. Baseline/rest phase is less definitive than evacuation. b: Sagittal MRI defecography during evacuation shows marked posterior compartment collapse with rectocele formation and associated enterocele, consistent with rectocele.
panels.attribution_text: Nobrega et al. Anterior-Only Sacrocolpopexy Complicated by Obstructive Enterocele: Should Both Compartments Always Be Repaired?. Cureus 2025. doi:10.7759/cureus.99038. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: MRI defecography, sagittal view. (a) At rest, anterior, middle, and posterior compartment descent measured relative to the pubococcygeal line (PCL): 1.9 cm, 3.4 cm, and 1.6 cm, respectively, demonstrating mild posterior descent. (b) During evacuation, descent below the PCL increases to 1.0 cm (anterior), 4.7 cm (middle), and 5.2 cm (posterior), revealing marked posterior compartment collapse with rectocele formation and an obstructive enterocele measuring 52.0 mm.
in_text_mentions: MRI defecography demonstrated a moderately severe enterocele with a small anterior rectocele, mild intrarectal intussusception, and obstructive descent of the small bowel into the rectovaginal space (Figure 2a, 2b). As no universally accepted radiological grading system exists for enterocele severity on dynamic MRI, severity was described based on the extent of small-bowel descent below the pubococcygeal line. These findings confirmed the suspicion of an obstructive enterocele explaining the patient’s defecatory dysfunction.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Real-patient sagittal dynamic MRI defecography image explicitly described as showing an anterior rectocele on the first evacuation attempt. [raw subtype: anterior rectocele] B: Real-patient sagittal dynamic MRI defecography image explicitly described as showing an anterior rectocele on the second evacuation attempt. [raw subtype: anterior rectocele] C: Real-patient sagittal dynamic MRI defecography image explicitly described as showing an anterior rectocele on the third evacuation attempt. [raw subtype: anterior rectocele] D: Real-patient sagittal dynamic MRI defecography image explicitly demonstrating underlying recto-rectal intussusception on the final evacuation, in the context of an anterior rectocele. [raw subtype: anterior rectocele with recto-rectal intussusception]
panels.attribution_text: Abdelatty et al. ESR Essentials: pelvic floor imaging-practice recommendations by the European Society of Urogenital Radiology.. European radiology 2026. doi:10.1007/s00330-026-12706-1. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: Sagittal FSP T2WI during repeated evacuation trials, demonstrating how the diagnosis evolves with each attempt and its impact on management. A–C Consecutive MRD images with the first three attempts show an anterior rectocele with a tight distal anal canal, whereas only the final evacuation (D) reveals the underlying recto-rectal intussusception. This case outlines the importance of repeating the evacuation phase at least three times in MRD to show hidden functional disorders
in_text_mentions: g straining (Fig. 2), ideally with gel seen traversing the anal canal lumen [16]. The evacuation sequence should be repeated until the rectum is fully emptied to rule out rectal intussusception (Fig. 3).
